Summary: What condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins, PACs) do to quercetin solubility in red wine
- Condensed tannins in red wine increase quercetin’s apparent solubility by forming noncovalent complexes (co‑pigmentation and hydrogen-bonding/pi–π stacking) with flavonols, but this solubilization is conditional on matrix composition, temperature, time, and phenolic reactivity; above supersaturation thresholds and under aging/oxidation, quercetin tends to precipitate as fine needles, often after initial complexation and protein trapping by high‑molecular‑weight tannin assemblies. <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Non‑covalent interactions between wine phenolics and quercetin can stabilize the flavonol in solution and increase its apparent solubility, with anthocyanin co‑pigmentation preventing immediate precipitation</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-1">Quercetin’s solubility mirrors that in simple hydroalcoholic solutions, with a precipitation risk rising once concentrations exceed about 3 mg/L and growing over time</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">Spiking quercetin into red wines yields substantially more solubilized flavonol than in hydroalcoholic buffer at 18 °C, and the effect is stronger in wines rich in bleachable pigments, consistent with quercetin sequestration into soluble complexes</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-3">High‑molecular‑weight tannins/procyanidins bind salivary proline‑rich proteins and form insoluble complexes that collect other phenolics, illustrating how tannin scaffolds create protein‑trapping, cross‑linked assemblies capable of sequestering flavonols</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-4">Copigmentation elevates quercetin solubility early, but these complexes can break down during storage, allowing precipitation</cite>.

1) Thermodynamic and kinetic drivers: thresholds, temperature, and time
- Quercetin aglycone is hydrophobic, with low water solubility; in wine, ethanol and pH modulate this, but typical alcoholic content alone does not fully explain the high apparent solubility observed in real reds relative to simple buffers. <cite id="fd4e9c19-1">Pharmaceutical/biologic solubility data show quercetin is poorly soluble (0.17–28.9 μg/mL across media), and in wine its solubility tracks that in hydroalcoholic solutions; importantly, about 3 mg/L (~300 μg/L) marks a critical concentration above which deposit formation becomes significant, with precipitation increasing over time</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-1">Deposits form faster in hydroalcoholic buffers than in real wines, where nucleation and growth are slowed by the complex matrix</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Solubility is lower at 0 °C than at 18 °C across matrices; the presence of anthocyanins increases soluble quercetin via co‑pigmentation</cite>.
- In practice, red wines rich in “bleachable pigments” (flavanol–anthocyanin adducts and phenolic polymers) maintain more quercetin in solution; as these pigments decline with oxidation or hydrolysis, quercetin release and haze emerge. <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">Solubilized quercetin at 18 °C was much lower in buffer than in wines; Barbera (high bleachable pigment) solubilized more quercetin than Sangiovese and Cirò, and quercetin content correlated positively with bleachable pigment content</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-4">Hydrolysis of quercetin glycosides releases the aglycone, raising supersaturation risk; oxidation and nucleation seeds accelerate precipitation</cite>.

2) How condensed tannins interact with quercetin: mechanisms and outcomes
- Direct complexation and solubilization: Tannin backbones (catechin/gallocatechin) provide sites for hydrogen‑bonding and π–π stacking with flavonol rings, reducing free quercetin concentration and delaying crystallization; anthocyanins can act as co‑pigmentors, often synergizing with tannins to keep quercetin soluble early in storage. <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Non‑covalent interactions between quercetin and anthocyanins form soluble co‑pigmentation complexes that inhibit quercetin precipitation</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Increasing anthocyanin levels in model solution corresponded to higher quercetin levels, confirming co‑pigmentation enhances solubility</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Wine matrices rich in flavonoids show moderate correlations between soluble quercetin after 8 months and measures of tannin/anthocyanin/flavan content, supporting macromolecular solubilization</cite>.
- Sequestration into high‑molecular‑weight colloids: In real wines, condensed tannins often polymerize into polymeric proanthocyanidin networks that bind proteins and other phenolics, forming macroscopic colloids that can encapsulate quercetin; this increases apparent solubility while preventing light scattering typical of free crystals. <cite id="fdf1dc13-3">Procyanidins and other high‑molecular‑weight tannins in aged wine showed high binding affinity to salivary proteins and formed insoluble complexes that collected other phenolics during precipitation, illustrating cross‑linking assembly of tannin scaffolds</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-3">Model‑to‑matrix extrapolation indicates tannin–protein complexes can remain soluble when decorated with polysaccharides, while tannin–protein aggregates can precipitate, underscoring that polymerization state and matrix determine quercetin fate</cite>.
- Oxidation, adduct formation, and release: As PACs oxidize and recombine, co‑polymerize, or form metal chelates (e.g., PAC–anthocyanin–metal), the microenvironment for sequestered quercetin changes; over months, complex breakdown and nucleation sites lead to quercetin release and haze. <cite id="fdf1dc13-1">The wine matrix’s pH, temperature, nucleation seeds, and phenolic composition govern quercetin stability; anthocyanin–flavonol complexes can become unstable with time, enabling precipitation</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-4">Oxidation and nucleation seeds accelerate quercetin precipitation from initially soluble states</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">Quercetin haze formation appears as anthocetin forms non‑bleachable pigments or degrades, implying release of quercetin from co‑pigmentation complexes during maturation</cite>.

3) Matrix effects in red wine: ethanol, pH, proteins, polysaccharides, oxygen, and varietal differences
- Ethanol and pH: Alcohol content in red wine modestly increases quercetin solubility, but the dominant effect arises from phenolic interactions and colloidal stabilization rather than ethanol alone. <cite id="fd4e9c19-1">Solubility increases with ethanol in water, yet wine solubility closely mirrors water, indicating alcohol alone is insufficient to control precipitation risk</cite>.
- Proteins and polysaccharides: Grape tannins interact with proteins and can be stabilized by polysaccharides; these interactions modulate colloidal stability and can prevent or promote aggregation depending on stoichiometry and matrix. <cite id="fd4e9c19-3">Tannins interact with proteins to precipitate or with polysaccharides to yield soluble colloids; free proteins can persist depending on matrix and ratios, and polysaccharides stabilize colloids</cite>.
- Tannin load and “bleachable pigments”: Wines with higher levels of iron‑reactive phenols, vanillin‑reactive flavans, and high tannin/anthocyanin ratios show more soluble quercetin and reduced haze growth. <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Soluble quercetin after 8 months correlates with vanillin‑reactive flavans, iron‑reactive phenols, protein‑reactive tannins, and tannin/monomeric anthocyanin ratios, supporting macromolecular facilitation of quercetin solubilization</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">Quercetin solubilization is higher in wines rich in bleachable pigments; correlation with bisulfite‑bleachable pigments explains higher quercetin levels</cite>.
- Oxygen, temperature, and seeds: Oxidative aging increases precipitation risk; low temperatures lower solubility; nucleation seeds catalyze crystal growth once supersaturation occurs. <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Solubility at 0 °C is lower than at 18 °C across matrices</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-4">Prolonged storage, oxidation, and nucleation seeds accelerate precipitation</cite>.
- Varietal and vintage drivers: Climate and UV exposure increase quercetin and glycoside precursors; varieties like Sangiovese are prone to deposits, yet quercetin levels alone do not predict precipitation absent matrix interactions. <cite id="fdf1dc13-1">UV‑B and climate change elevate quercetin biosynthesis, increasing the likelihood of exceeding solubility thresholds</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-4">Quercetin glycosides hydrolyze to aglycone during fermentation/ageing, elevating supersaturation risk</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-4">Sangiovese commonly shows quercetin deposits despite high quercetin content, highlighting the role of matrix and time</cite>.

4) From reaction to observable outcomes in red wine
- Early wine: Interactions with PACs and anthocyanins produce soluble quercetin–phenolic complexes that resist light scattering and crystal growth; total quercetin (glycosides plus aglycone) remains elevated, but haze is absent. <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">Red wines hold much more solubilized quercetin than buffer, with Barbera showing markedly higher solubilization than others, consistent with complexation</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Co‑pigmentation with anthocyanins maintains quercetin in solution and inhibits immediate precipitation</cite>.
- Mid‑ to long‑term evolution: Oxidation of anthocyanins and PACs, protein binding and aggregation, and polymer growth reduce complex stability; quercetin can be released, reach supersaturation (>3 mg/L), and nucleate, producing needle‑shaped haze and deposits, especially at lower temperatures. <cite id="fdf1dc13-4">Supersaturation above ~3 mg/L increases deposit risk; oxidation and nucleation seeds accelerate precipitation</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">As anthocyanins degrade or become non‑bleachable, quercetin is released from co‑pigmentation complexes, causing haze formation</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-3">High‑DP tannins form protein‑trapping insoluble complexes that collect other phenolics in aged wine, consistent with complex rearrangements and eventual precipitation</cite>.
- Quantitative benchmarks: Field and model studies converge on 3 mg/L as a practical threshold and show slower nucleation in real wines due to matrix stabilization, though exact solubility varies with composition and time. <cite id="fd4e9c19-1">A critical concentration of ~3 mg/L marks significant deposit formation risk, with time‑dependent precipitation</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">Deposits take longer to form in real wines than in hydroalcoholic buffers, with wine matrix increasing solubility relative to simple solutions</cite>.

5) Practical implications for winemaking and sensory quality
- Composition management: Tannin management (extraction control, microoxygenation, enzyme/adsorbent interventions) and antioxidant measures can reduce supersaturation and stabilize quercetin–tannin complexes; however, each approach risks collateral effects on color, aroma, and overall colloidal stability. <cite id="fd4e9c19-3">Strategies include removing quercetin below solubility thresholds via PVPP/charcoal/yeast lysates, microoxygenation to hydrolyze glycosides and promote controlled precipitation (nucleation seeding), but trade‑offs with color/aroma stability must be considered</cite>.
- Prediction and monitoring: Current practice relies on HPLC, but rapid tests are needed; correlations between quercetin solubility and “bleachable pigments” and tannin indices offer practical proxies. <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Soluble quercetin correlates with iron‑reactive phenols, vanillin‑reactive flavans, protein‑reactive tannins, and tannin/anthocyanin ratios</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-3">HPLC is accurate but not practical for routine production; development of rapid tests is a key unmet need</cite>.

6) What we know and key uncertainties
- Known: Condensed tannins increase quercetin’s apparent solubility via noncovalent complexation and sequestration into high‑molecular‑weight phenolic/protein assemblies; precipitation risk escalates when concentrations exceed ~3 mg/L and with aging, oxidation, and low temperature; wine matrix (anthocyanins, tannins, proteins, sugars, acids) modulates nucleation and growth. <cite id="fd4e9c19-1">Noncovalent interactions and a 3 mg/L threshold govern precipitation risk</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Anthocyanin co‑pigmentation prevents immediate precipitation and soluble quercetin increases with anthocyanin levels</cite> <cite id="fdf1dc13-3">High‑DP tannins form protein‑trapping insoluble complexes that collect other phenolics in aged wine</cite>.
- Uncertainties: Direct, quantitative binding constants between quercetin and defined PAC subunits (DP 3–6, catechin vs gallocatechin) in wine‑relevant matrices remain sparse; spectroscopic mapping of quercetin–PAC hydrogen‑bonding vs π–π stacking contributions under ethanol/pH gradients is limited; long‑term evolution of quercetin within PAC–protein–anthocyanin supercomplexes under microperoxidase conditions needs deeper study. <cite id="fd4e9c19-0">Reviews emphasize the need to exploit quercetin’s interactions with other phenolic compounds and integrate new analytical tools</cite>.

Practical takeaway: In red wine, condensed tannins act as colloidal “sponges” that transiently solubilize quercetin through noncovalent complexation and sequestration, raising apparent solubility and suppressing haze; with aging, oxidation, and matrix depletion, quercetin can be released, reach supersaturation, and precipitate as fine needles. Wineries manage this by balancing extraction, oxygen control, matrix composition, and nucleation seeding to keep quercetin below precipitation thresholds while preserving sensory quality. <cite id="fd4e9c19-1">The ~3 mg/L threshold and time‑dependence provide practical targets</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-2">Matrix enrichment in bleachable pigments and anthocyanins increases solubilized quercetin; their decline correlates with haze emergence</cite> <cite id="fd4e9c19-3">High‑molecular‑weight tannin assemblies bind proteins and other phenolics, explaining both solubilization and later precipitation dynamics</cite>.

Title: Red Wine Colloids: Advances in Characterization and Strategies for Colloidal Stability
Snippet: Colloidal aggregation in red wines has historically been linked to the well-known interaction between tannins and proteins. For decades, it was commonly believed that proteins would not be present in red wines because the extraction of large quantities of phenolic compounds during maceration would lead to their complete precipitation. Indeed, early models for colloidal aggregation in red wines incorporated this concept, as postulated by Saucier 74 (Figure 2A). According to the first model, flavanol molecules extracted during maceration first interact with one another through hydrophobic interactions, forming colloidal flavanol particles. These particles can then either react with wine proteins via van der Waals interactions and precipitate or interact with polysaccharides to form stable solutions. Therefore, although the model did not account for the presence of free proteins in red wines, it has the merit of highlighting the involvement and importance of wine polysaccharides for the stabilization of colloidal particles. 

Almost a decade later, Portuguese researchers, using model systems, attempted to better understand how wine macromolecules interact to form different colloidal particles 69 (Figure 2B). Using individual colloid-forming molecules, they hypothesized that tannins interacting with proteins result in a precipitate (insoluble complex), whereas tannins interacting with polysaccharides yield soluble colloidal particles. They also reported that, in some cases, not all proteins participate in precipitation with tannins; this behavior largely depends on the wine matrix and on the protein-to-tannin ratio. Indeed, their results indicate that proteins may exist in free form in red  wines, while protein-tannin aggregates may also remain soluble when interacting with polysaccharides to form a ternary complex. These findings also shed light on the affinity of tannins for proteins, although the conclusions were drawn from relatively simple model systems rather than real wines. 

As research progressed, it became clear that the molecular interactions in real wines are far more complex than those in model solutions, as numerous compounds and wine parameters can affect the reactivity of the individual colloid-forming molecules.
</snippet>

Title: Quercetin instability in red wines: Insights into precipitation and control approaches
Snippet: The instability of flavonols represents one of the most pressing oenological challenges today for red wines. The aglycone form of quercetin is poorly soluble, favouring its precipitation as crystals and leading to the formation of undesirable deposits that compromise the visual appearance and commercial value of wines. Initially reported sporadically and mainly in varieties such as Sangiovese, this phenomenon has become increasingly common, likely due to climate change and higher solar radiation influencing flavonol biosynthesis. The complexity of the wine matrix, a colloidal system involving numerous non-covalent interactions, makes it difficult to predict and control quercetin solubility and precipitation.

Title: Quercetin instability in red wines: Insights into precipitation and control approaches
Snippet: One of the fields in which numerous studies of solubility has been carried out is the pharmaceutical. Quercetin being a hydrophobic molecule has relatively low solubility in water (0.17-7 μg/mL), gastric fluids (5.5 μg/mL), and small intestine fluids (28.9 μg/mL) (Kandemir et al., 2022;Kasikci & Bagdatlioglu, 2016). Consequently, this low solubility leads to a tendency for quercetin to precipitate in these fluids, which diminishes its bio-accessibility and, therefore, the amount available for absorption. In wine we have firstly to consider that pH and ethanol affect quercetin solubility. Previous investigations by Abraham et al. (2014) demonstrated that the solubility of quercetin increases proportionally with the ethanol concentration in aqueous solutions. Interestingly, the solubility of quercetin in wine closely mirrors that observed in water, suggesting that the ethanol content is too low to govern quercetin solubility in such matrices. In a more recent study, Gambuti et al. (2020) conducted an in-depth assessment of the solubility and precipitation thresholds of quercetin in both hydroalcoholic solutions and red wines. The authors identified 3 mg/L as a critical concentration above which the risk of quercetin deposit formation becomes significant. Title: Red Wine Colloids: Advances in Characterization and Strategies for Colloidal Stability
Snippet: Colloidal aggregation in red wines has historically been linked to the well-known interaction between tannins and proteins. For decades, it was commonly believed that proteins would not be present in red wines because the extraction of large quantities of phenolic compounds during maceration would lead to their complete precipitation. Indeed, early models for colloidal aggregation in red wines incorporated this concept, as postulated by Saucier 74 (Figure 2A). According to the first model, flavanol molecules extracted during maceration first interact with one another through hydrophobic interactions, forming colloidal flavanol particles. These particles can then either react with wine proteins via van der Waals interactions and precipitate or interact with polysaccharides to form stable solutions. Therefore, although the model did not account for the presence of free proteins in red wines, it has the merit of highlighting the involvement and importance of wine polysaccharides for the stabilization of colloidal particles. 

Almost a decade later, Portuguese researchers, using model systems, attempted to better understand how wine macromolecules interact to form different colloidal particles 69 (Figure 2B). Using individual colloid-forming molecules, they hypothesized that tannins interacting with proteins result in a precipitate (insoluble complex), whereas tannins interacting with polysaccharides yield soluble colloidal particles. They also reported that, in some cases, not all proteins participate in precipitation with tannins; this behavior largely depends on the wine matrix and on the protein-to-tannin ratio. Indeed, their results indicate that proteins may exist in free form in red  wines, while protein-tannin aggregates may also remain soluble when interacting with polysaccharides to form a ternary complex. These findings also shed light on the affinity of tannins for proteins, although the conclusions were drawn from relatively simple model systems rather than real wines. 

As research progressed, it became clear that the molecular interactions in real wines are far more complex than those in model solutions, as numerous compounds and wine parameters can affect the reactivity of the individual colloid-forming molecules.

snippet.text: One of the fields in which numerous studies of solubility has been carried out is the pharmaceutical. Quercetin being a hydrophobic molecule has relatively low solubility in water (0.17-7 μg/mL), gastric fluids (5.5 μg/mL), and small intestine fluids (28.9 μg/mL) (Kandemir et al., 2022;Kasikci & Bagdatlioglu, 2016). Consequently, this low solubility leads to a tendency for quercetin to precipitate in these fluids, which diminishes its bio-accessibility and, therefore, the amount available for absorption. In wine we have firstly to consider that pH and ethanol affect quercetin solubility. Previous investigations by Abraham et al. (2014) demonstrated that the solubility of quercetin increases proportionally with the ethanol concentration in aqueous solutions. Interestingly, the solubility of quercetin in wine closely mirrors that observed in water, suggesting that the ethanol content is too low to govern quercetin solubility in such matrices. In a more recent study, Gambuti et al. (2020) conducted an in-depth assessment of the solubility and precipitation thresholds of quercetin in both hydroalcoholic solutions and red wines. The authors identified 3 mg/L as a critical concentration above which the risk of quercetin deposit formation becomes significant. Notably, they also highlighted the temporal dependence of quercetin precipitation, indicating that deposit formation increases over time. In agreement with findings of Chebil et al. (2007), the medium in  which quercetin is dissolved plays a crucial role in modulating its precipitation. Unlike simple hydroalcoholic solutions, wine represents a complex colloidal system in which several components may affect the nucleation and growth of quercetin crystals. Moreover, non-covalent interactions could contribute to the stabilization of quercetin in solution increasing its solubility.

Title: Quercetin instability in red wines: Insights into precipitation and control approaches
Snippet: The instability of flavonols represents one of the most pressing oenological challenges today for red wines. The aglycone form of quercetin is poorly soluble, favouring its precipitation as crystals and leading to the formation of undesirable deposits that compromise the visual appearance and commercial value of wines. Initially reported sporadically and mainly in varieties such as Sangiovese, this phenomenon has become increasingly common, likely due to climate change and higher solar radiation influencing flavonol biosynthesis. The complexity of the wine matrix, a colloidal system involving numerous non-covalent interactions, makes it difficult to predict and control quercetin solubility and precipitation. 

A deeper understanding of the mechanisms governing the extraction, evolution and precipitation of quercetin is essential for developing targeted, sustainable winemaking protocols. Looking ahead, it will be crucial to integrate this knowledge with new analytical tools and innovative strategies, including those aimed at enhancing quercetin solubility or exploiting its interactions with other phenolic compounds. 

Several strategies have been suggested to address the flavonol instability in finished wines. These include approaches aimed at removing quercetin aglycone and its glycosides below its solubility threshold by using oenological additives as PVPP, charcoal or yeast lysates, or by using specific enzymes with glycosidic activity or by microoxygenation to decrease the amount of free aglycon and promoting controlled precipitation prior to bottling using nucleation seeding. However, the potential side effects of each approach on colour, aroma, and overall wine stability must be carefully evaluated and none of these approaches until now used can be considered as free of collateral effect. 

Looking for future studies, investigations in different areas could be considered. Here are listed the main research lines that should be more deepen in future works. 

(1) Development of a rapid and simple test to predict quercetin instability in wines. 

A key challenge in managing quercetin precipitation is the lack of practical, rapid analytical tools available to wineries. Although current quantification methods, mainly HPLC-UV methods, are accurate, they are also time-consuming and expensive, making them impractical for routine use during production.

Title: Influence of matter other than grapes on quercetin evolution and wine polyphenols
Snippet: Quercetin precipitation is a phenomenon that primarily occurs in red wines and, to a lesser extent, in white wines (Somers & Ziemelis, 1985;Ziemelis & Pickering, 1969). Quercetin is a flavonol naturally present in grapes. Under certain conditions, it becomes insoluble and forms needle-shaped crystals that cause turbidity and undesirable deposits (Gambuti et al., 2020;Luciano et al., 2024). This issue, which significantly impacts wine quality, has garnered considerable attention. 

Factors influencing quercetin precipitation include the hydrolysis of quercetin glycosides during fermentation and ageing, which releases quercetin aglycone, a compound with low solubility in hydroalcoholic solutions, particularly at low temperatures (Lanati et al., 2021;Lanati et al., 2022;Li et al., 2013;McDonald et al., 1998). Supersaturation of quercetin aglycone, with concentrations exceeding 3 mg/L, also poses a significant risk of precipitation (Gambuti et al., 2020;Srinivas et al., 2010). Grape-related factors such as variety (e.g., Sangiovese), sunlight exposure, and water stress influence the accumulation of quercetin and its precursors (Gambuti et al., 2020;Ojeda et al., 2002;Price et al., 1995;Vendramin et al., 2022). Moreover, copigmentation with anthocyanins initially increases quercetin solubility, but the instability of these complexes can lead to precipitation over time (Lanati et al., 2022;Luciano et al., 2024). Other contributing factors include low temperatures, prolonged storage, oxidation, and nucleation seeds, which further accelerate quercetin precipitation (Castellari et al., 2000;Castellari et al., 2001;Lanati et al., 2022;Luciano et al., 2024).

snippet.text: One of the fields in which numerous studies of solubility has been carried out is the pharmaceutical. Quercetin being a hydrophobic molecule has relatively low solubility in water (0.17-7 μg/mL), gastric fluids (5.5 μg/mL), and small intestine fluids (28.9 μg/mL) (Kandemir et al., 2022;Kasikci & Bagdatlioglu, 2016). Consequently, this low solubility leads to a tendency for quercetin to precipitate in these fluids, which diminishes its bio-accessibility and, therefore, the amount available for absorption. In wine we have firstly to consider that pH and ethanol affect quercetin solubility. Previous investigations by Abraham et al. (2014) demonstrated that the solubility of quercetin increases proportionally with the ethanol concentration in aqueous solutions. Interestingly, the solubility of quercetin in wine closely mirrors that observed in water, suggesting that the ethanol content is too low to govern quercetin solubility in such matrices. In a more recent study, Gambuti et al. (2020) conducted an in-depth assessment of the solubility and precipitation thresholds of quercetin in both hydroalcoholic solutions and red wines. The authors identified 3 mg/L as a critical concentration above which the risk of quercetin deposit formation becomes significant. Notably, they also highlighted the temporal dependence of quercetin precipitation, indicating that deposit formation increases over time. In agreement with findings of Chebil et al. (2007), the medium in  which quercetin is dissolved plays a crucial role in modulating its precipitation. Unlike simple hydroalcoholic solutions, wine represents a complex colloidal system in which several components may affect the nucleation and growth of quercetin crystals. Moreover, non-covalent interactions could contribute to the stabilization of quercetin in solution increasing its solubility.

snippet.text:
The instability of flavonols represents one of the most pressing oenological challenges today for red wines. The aglycone form of quercetin is poorly soluble, favouring its precipitation as crystals and leading to the formation of undesirable deposits that compromise the visual appearance and commercial value of wines. Initially reported sporadically and mainly in varieties such as Sangiovese, this phenomenon has become increasingly common, likely due to climate change and higher solar radiation influencing flavonol biosynthesis. The complexity of the wine matrix, a colloidal system involving numerous non-covalent interactions, makes it difficult to predict and control quercetin solubility and precipitation. 

A deeper understanding of the mechanisms governing the extraction, evolution and precipitation of quercetin is essential for developing targeted, sustainable winemaking protocols. Looking ahead, it will be crucial to integrate this knowledge with new analytical tools and innovative strategies, including those aimed at enhancing quercetin solubility or exploiting its interactions with other phenolic compounds. 

Several strategies have been suggested to address the flavonol instability in finished wines. These include approaches aimed at removing quercetin aglycone and its glycosides below its solubility threshold by using oenological additives as PVPP, charcoal or yeast lysates, or by using specific enzymes with glycosidic activity or by microoxygenation to decrease the amount of free aglycon and promoting controlled precipitation prior to bottling using nucleation seeding. However, the potential side effects of each approach on colour, aroma, and overall wine stability must be carefully evaluated and none of these approaches until now used can be considered as free of collateral effect. 

Looking for future studies, investigations in different areas could be considered. Here are listed the main research lines that should be more deepen in future works. 

(1) Development of a rapid and simple test to predict quercetin instability in wines. 

A key challenge in managing quercetin precipitation is the lack of practical, rapid analytical tools available to wineries. Although current quantification methods, mainly HPLC-UV methods, are accurate, they are also time-consuming and expensive, making them impractical for routine use during production.

snippet.text:
Quercetin precipitation is a phenomenon that primarily occurs in red wines and, to a lesser extent, in white wines (Somers & Ziemelis, 1985;Ziemelis & Pickering, 1969). Quercetin is a flavonol naturally present in grapes. Under certain conditions, it becomes insoluble and forms needle-shaped crystals that cause turbidity and undesirable deposits (Gambuti et al., 2020;Luciano et al., 2024). This issue, which significantly impacts wine quality, has garnered considerable attention. 

Factors influencing quercetin precipitation include the hydrolysis of quercetin glycosides during fermentation and ageing, which releases quercetin aglycone, a compound with low solubility in hydroalcoholic solutions, particularly at low temperatures (Lanati et al., 2021;Lanati et al., 2022;Li et al., 2013;McDonald et al., 1998). Supersaturation of quercetin aglycone, with concentrations exceeding 3 mg/L, also poses a significant risk of precipitation (Gambuti et al., 2020;Srinivas et al., 2010). Grape-related factors such as variety (e.g., Sangiovese), sunlight exposure, and water stress influence the accumulation of quercetin and its precursors (Gambuti et al., 2020;Ojeda et al., 2002;Price et al., 1995;Vendramin et al., 2022). Moreover, copigmentation with anthocyanins initially increases quercetin solubility, but the instability of these complexes can lead to precipitation over time (Lanati et al., 2022;Luciano et al., 2024). Other contributing factors include low temperatures, prolonged storage, oxidation, and nucleation seeds, which further accelerate quercetin precipitation (Castellari et al., 2000;Castellari et al., 2001;Lanati et al., 2022;Luciano et al., 2024).

Title: Quercetin instability in red wines: Insights into precipitation and control approaches
Snippet: One effect of climate change on grape composition is the increased biosynthesis of quercetin and its glycosides in response to UV-B radiation. High concentrations of quercetin in wine can exceed its solubility threshold, resulting in undesirable precipitation that negatively impacts clarity and consumer perception. This poses a challenge to producers in terms of both quality and economics. Starting from a survey of quercetin instability and its presence in wines, this review summarises the current understanding of the biochemical and physicochemical mechanisms that regulate quercetin stability and precipitation in red wines. It also covers the factors involved in quercetin extraction and stability during vinification and oenological strategies to counteract these effects. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the stability of quercetin in red wines is governed by a complex interplay of factors, including anthocyanin-mediated copigmentation, pH, temperature, nucleation seeds and the broader phenolic composition of the wine matrix. By elucidating these mechanisms, the review provides a framework for predicting and managing quercetin precipitation, thereby supporting improved wine quality and colloidal stability in the challenging conditions imposed by climate change.

Title: Procyanidins and Anthocyanins in Young and Aged Prokupac Wines: Evaluation of Their Reactivity Toward Salivary Proteins
Snippet: Interestingly, the results of the binding affinity of anthocyanins in young and aged wines showed significant differences. Anthocyanins in young wine showed little or no binding affinity for salivary proteins (0 to 15.86%). Previous studies have also indicated that poor electrostatic (ionic) interactions between anthocyanins and salivary proteins [24,33] and the formation of soluble aggregates (Figure 4a) contribute to the perception of astringency [26]. On the other hand, the same anthocyanins and vitisin B in aged wine were almost completely retained in the precipitate, apparently showing a "high" binding affinity. This can also be explained by the fact that the contents of total and individual anthocyanins in APW were significantly lower than in YPW (Table S2). For example, the content of malvidin 3-O-glucoside was almost 8-fold lower in APW than in YPW (Table 2). As aforementioned, these differences in the binding affinities of selected phenolics (epicatechin, procyanidins, and anthocyanins) can be explained by the different compositions of young and aged wines (Tables 1 and 2), as well as by the synergistic effects of other wine phenolics [33]. In the case of aged Prokupac wine, procyanidins, high-molecular-weight tannins, and ellagitannins showed high binding affinities for salivary proteins [19,21,30,38] and formed insoluble complexes that probably collected and intensively bound other phenolics during precipitation. The results of the targeted analysis supported the conclusions and results of the electrophoretic analyses. 

Taking into account previous interpretations [33,[54][55][56][57] and the results of this study, the mechanism of interactions between proline-rich proteins and the major wine phenolics is illustrated (Figure 4a), along with a schematic representation of the formation of insoluble complexes between PRPs and phenolic compounds in young (Figure 4b) and aged (Figure 4c) wines.

snippet.text:
Quercetin precipitation is a phenomenon that primarily occurs in red wines and, to a lesser extent, in white wines (Somers & Ziemelis, 1985;Ziemelis & Pickering, 1969). Quercetin is a flavonol naturally present in grapes. Under certain conditions, it becomes insoluble and forms needle-shaped crystals that cause turbidity and undesirable deposits (Gambuti et al., 2020;Luciano et al., 2024). This issue, which significantly impacts wine quality, has garnered considerable attention. 

Factors influencing quercetin precipitation include the hydrolysis of quercetin glycosides during fermentation and ageing, which releases quercetin aglycone, a compound with low solubility in hydroalcoholic solutions, particularly at low temperatures (Lanati et al., 2021;Lanati et al., 2022;Li et al., 2013;McDonald et al., 1998). Supersaturation of quercetin aglycone, with concentrations exceeding 3 mg/L, also poses a significant risk of precipitation (Gambuti et al., 2020;Srinivas et al., 2010). Grape-related factors such as variety (e.g., Sangiovese), sunlight exposure, and water stress influence the accumulation of quercetin and its precursors (Gambuti et al., 2020;Ojeda et al., 2002;Price et al., 1995;Vendramin et al., 2022). Moreover, copigmentation with anthocyanins initially increases quercetin solubility, but the instability of these complexes can lead to precipitation over time (Lanati et al., 2022;Luciano et al., 2024). Other contributing factors include low temperatures, prolonged storage, oxidation, and nucleation seeds, which further accelerate quercetin precipitation (Castellari et al., 2000;Castellari et al., 2001;Lanati et al., 2022;Luciano et al., 2024).

documents.snippet:
Moreover, non-covalent interactions could contribute to the stabilization of quercetin in solution increasing its solubility. Lanati et al. (2022) evaluated the solubility of quercetin in hydroalcoholic buffer solution, in three different red wines, and in a white wine, by spiking them with 30 mg/L of quercetin and considering different storage temperatures. They observed that solubility was lower at 0 • C compared to 18 • C in all cases. Additionally, results suggested that an observed higher solubility of quercetin in wines can be due to the presence of anthocyanins, which may help to maintain quercetin in solution. The formation of soluble co-pigmentation complexes between quercetin and anthocyanins could prevent quercetin precipitation. These significant findings were confirmed by a recent study (Luciano et al., 2024), which evaluated the effect of increasing anthocyanin concentrations on quercetin solubility in a model solution. 

The results showed that higher concentrations of anthocyanins in solution corresponded to higher concentrations of quercetin in solution. 

Another important finding was that this effect decreases over time. A significant contribution to this idea was made by Borghini (2022), who screened over 50 Sangiovese samples from various vintages. The study identified significant positive correlations between quercetin aglycone and anthocyanins, as well as between the bound forms of quercetin and tannins. These findings were partially confirmed by Luciano et al., (2025), who carried out a correlation test on 32 red wines from the 2023 vintage and found a moderate correlation between the amount of soluble quercetin after 8 months of bottle storage and flavonoids detected as vanillin reactive flavans, iron-reactive phenols, bovine serum albumine-reactive tannins and the ratios tannins/monomeric anthocyanins and flavans/monomeric anthocyanins supporting the hypothesis that the presence of these macromolecules may facilitate the solubilization of quercetin and inhibit crystal growth. (Luciano et al., 2025).

documents.title: Quercetin instability in red wines: Insights into precipitation and control approaches
documents.snippet: One effect of climate change on grape composition is the increased biosynthesis of quercetin and its glycosides in response to UV-B radiation. High concentrations of quercetin in wine can exceed its solubility threshold, resulting in undesirable precipitation that negatively impacts clarity and consumer perception. This poses a challenge to producers in terms of both quality and economics. Starting from a survey of quercetin instability and its presence in wines, this review summarises the current understanding of the biochemical and physicochemical mechanisms that regulate quercetin stability and precipitation in red wines. It also covers the factors involved in quercetin extraction and stability during vinification and oenological strategies to counteract these effects. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the stability of quercetin in red wines is governed by a complex interplay of factors, including anthocyanin-mediated copigmentation, pH, temperature, nucleation seeds and the broader phenolic composition of the wine matrix. By elucidating these mechanisms, the review provides a framework for predicting and managing quercetin precipitation, thereby supporting improved wine quality and colloidal stability in the challenging conditions imposed by climate change.

documents.title: Quercetin instability in red wines: Insights into precipitation and control approaches
documents.snippet:
The instability of flavonols represents one of the most pressing oenological challenges today for red wines. The aglycone form of quercetin is poorly soluble, favouring its precipitation as crystals and leading to the formation of undesirable deposits that compromise the visual appearance and commercial value of wines. Initially reported sporadically and mainly in varieties such as Sangiovese, this phenomenon has become increasingly common, likely due to climate change and higher solar radiation influencing flavonol biosynthesis. The complexity of the wine matrix, a colloidal system involving numerous non-covalent interactions, makes it difficult to predict and control quercetin solubility and precipitation. 

A deeper understanding of the mechanisms governing the extraction, evolution and precipitation of quercetin is essential for developing targeted, sustainable winemaking protocols. Looking ahead, it will be crucial to integrate this knowledge with new analytical tools and innovative strategies, including those aimed at enhancing quercetin solubility or exploiting its interactions with other phenolic compounds. 

Several strategies have been suggested to address the flavonol instability in finished wines. These include approaches aimed at removing quercetin aglycone and its glycosides below its solubility threshold by using oenological additives as PVPP, charcoal or yeast lysates, or by using specific enzymes with glycosidic activity or by microoxygenation to decrease the amount of free aglycon and promoting controlled precipitation prior to bottling using nucleation seeding. However, the potential side effects of each approach on colour, aroma, and overall wine stability must be carefully evaluated and none of these approaches until now used can be considered as free of collateral effect. 

Looking for future studies, investigations in different areas could be considered. Here are listed the main research lines that should be more deepen in future works. 

(1) Development of a rapid and simple test to predict quercetin instability in wines. 

A key challenge in managing quercetin precipitation is the lack of practical, rapid analytical tools available to wineries. Although current quantification methods, mainly HPLC-UV methods, are accurate, they are also time-consuming and expensive, making them impractical for routine use during production.

documents.title: Procyanidins and Anthocyanins in Young and Aged Prokupac Wines: Evaluation of Their Reactivity Toward Salivary Proteins
documents.snippet:
Interestingly, the results of the binding affinity of anthocyanins in young and aged wines showed significant differences. Anthocyanins in young wine showed little or no binding affinity for salivary proteins (0 to 15.86%). Previous studies have also indicated that poor electrostatic (ionic) interactions between anthocyanins and salivary proteins [24,33] and the formation of soluble aggregates (Figure 4a) contribute to the perception of astringency [26]. On the other hand, the same anthocyanins and vitisin B in aged wine were almost completely retained in the precipitate, apparently showing a "high" binding affinity. This can also be explained by the fact that the contents of total and individual anthocyanins in APW were significantly lower than in YPW (Table S2). For example, the content of malvidin 3-O-glucoside was almost 8-fold lower in APW than in YPW (Table 2). As aforementioned, these differences in the binding affinities of selected phenolics (epicatechin, procyanidins, and anthocyanins) can be explained by the different compositions of young and aged wines (Tables 1 and 2), as well as by the synergistic effects of other wine phenolics [33]. In the case of aged Prokupac wine, procyanidins, high-molecular-weight tannins, and ellagitannins showed high binding affinities for salivary proteins [19,21,30,38] and formed insoluble complexes that probably collected and intensively bound other phenolics during precipitation. The results of the targeted analysis supported the conclusions and results of the electrophoretic analyses. 

Taking into account previous interpretations [33,[54][55][56][57] and the results of this study, the mechanism of interactions between proline-rich proteins and the major wine phenolics is illustrated (Figure 4a), along with a schematic representation of the formation of insoluble complexes between PRPs and phenolic compounds in young (Figure 4b) and aged (Figure 4c) wines.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins) do not generally increase the free aqueous concentration of quercetin, but they can increase quercetin’s apparent solubility by forming soluble complexes and copigmentation assemblies with other phenolics in wine matrices, thereby suppressing precipitation and shifting quercetin from free monomer toward bound species that remain in solution. In red wine, “solubility” is rarely a thermodynamic free-concentration question; it is typically an apparent measure of total quercetin-related species detectable spectrophotometrically or by binding equilibria, because noncovalent complexes with anthocyanins and tannins absorb differently and contribute to “in solution” mass without free quercetin monomer precipitating. <cite id="320002e8-0">Non‑covalent interactions with anthocyanins and wine phenolics can stabilize quercetin in solution and increase its apparent solubility</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Quercetin’s risk of precipitation depends on matrix composition, time, and concentration, with reports of a critical threshold around 3 mg/L and clear evidence that wine components modulate nucleation and growth via noncovalent interactions</cite>.

What “solubility” means in red wine
In wine chemistry, “solubility” of quercetin is often operationalized as the total amount “in solution” (free quercetin plus quercetin–phenolic complexes) rather than the thermodynamic solubility of the unbound flavonol. Spectrophotometric color indices and copigmentation metrics reflect total quercetin-related absorbance that arises from bound complexes, not just free quercetin. <cite id="2af35bf7-0">Copigmentation constants K1 for anthocyanin–quercetin complexes are on the order of 10^3 L/mol, indicating strong complex formation that contributes to color, whereas catechin and procyanidin interactions are weaker</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Experiments that spike quercetin into wine and track dissolution/precipitation show higher apparent solubility when anthocyanins and wine matrices are present, attributed to stabilizing complexes preventing quercetin precipitation</cite>. Because quercetin is relatively hydrophobic and phenolic matrices are complex, measurements in real wine differ from simple aqueous solubility and must account for binding to anthocyanins, tannins, acids, and metalloids. <cite id="320002e8-3">Quercetin’s intrinsic water solubility is low (μg/mL), but wine matrices and ethanol/pH modulate its apparent solubility and precipitation risk</cite>.

How condensed tannins affect quercetin
Mechanisms: binding, complexation, and copigmentation
Condensed tannins primarily act through noncovalent forces (π–π stacking, H-bonding, hydrophobic interactions) to complex phenolic chromophores and stabilize colored species. Direct copigmentation with anthocyanins by condensed tannins is generally less effective than with hydrolysable tannins or quercetin, but interactions can still occur and alter color expression and stability. <cite id="b9844c0a-0">In model wine, oenological tannins increased color (a*, decreased L* and b*), with hydrolysable tannins outperforming condensed tannins in copigmentation effectiveness by ~2–4×</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-4">Procyanidin dimers (B1/B2) showed weak copigmentation in model wine at typical concentrations, implying limited direct impact on color via copigmentation at physiologically relevant levels</cite>. When quercetin is present, it can participate in anthocyanin–quercetin–flavanol ternary complexes and act as a stabilizer over time, sometimes even suppressing catechin’s stabilizing role. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Quercetin‑3‑β‑D‑glucoside produced immediate copigmentation and greater stabilization over time; in the presence of quercetin, (+)‑catechin binding to malvidin was less effective, indicating quercetin–anthocyanin complexes can dominate and reduce catechin’s contribution</cite>.

Apparent solubility of quercetin in the presence of condensed tannins
Evidence from wine and model systems indicates that adding phenolic cofactors (including condensed tannins) raises the apparent solubility window for quercetin by forming soluble complexes, which delays or prevents free quercetin precipitation. <cite id="320002e8-0">A spike‑and‑store study showed that higher anthocyanin concentrations corresponded to higher quercetin concentrations remaining in solution, and that anthocyanin–quercetin copigmentation complexes prevent quercetin precipitation</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Subsequent work confirmed that hydrolysable tannins and wine matrices increase quercetin solubility via noncovalent interactions</cite>. Real‑wine correlations further support this: bound quercetin correlates with tannins and monomeric anthocyanins/flavanols, consistent with sequestration into complexes. <cite id="320002e8-0">Screening of Sangiovese wines found significant positive correlations between quercetin aglycone and anthocyanins, and between bound quercetin and tannins</cite>. At the same time, free quercetin can decrease over time as it binds to matrix components, and precipitation risk increases once dissolved quercetin exceeds a threshold (≈3 mg/L) and as tannin/anthocyanin levels decline with aging. <cite id="320002e8-0">Quercetin deposits were observed when solution content fell below ~3 mg/L, and the effect decreased over time as complexation shifted equilibria</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Deposits formed over time and increased above ~3 mg/L, with wine components modulating nucleation and growth via noncovalent interactions</cite>.

Condensed tannins vs hydrolysable tannins and quercetin: a hierarchy of effects
Quercetin itself is a stronger copigment and complex former than condensed tannins when interacting with anthocyanins, and even stronger than most flavanols; hydrolysable tannins (gallotannins/ellagitannins) often outperform condensed tannins in anthocyanin copigmentation in model wine. <cite id="b9844c0a-0">Hydrolysable tannins were 2–4× more effective copigments than condensed tannins in malvidin models, with effects that were dose‑ and pH/ethanol‑dependent</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-0">Anthocyanin–quercetin copigmentation had K1 ≈ 2900 ± 1300 L/mol, far exceeding catechin (≈90 ± 20 L/mol) and procyanidin dimers (≈330 ± 30 L/mol)</cite>. Thus, in the presence of quercetin, condensed tannins tend to bind to anthocyanins and/or to quercetin–anthocyanin complexes, potentially reducing free quercetin while increasing the apparent solubility (total bound + free) of quercetin‑related species. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Quercetin–anthocyanin complexes can dominate over catechin in stabilizing color over time, indicating that condensed tannins may bind to complexes and shift quercetin from free to bound pools</cite>.

Time, matrix composition, and concentration effects
Because quercetin’s solubility is matrix‑ and time‑dependent, the net effect of adding condensed tannins is not a simple increase in free quercetin. Instead, tannins can (i) form quercetin–tannin complexes that remain dissolved, increasing apparent solubility; (ii) drive anthocyanin–quercetin copigmentation that sequesters quercetin, lowering free quercetin; and (iii) contribute to long‑term precipitation risk if tannin levels decline or if dissolved quercetin exceeds ~3 mg/L. <cite id="320002e8-0">Higher anthocyanin concentrations maintained more quercetin in solution via copigmentation, but this effect diminished over time</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">A threshold around 3 mg/L marked the onset of significant deposit formation, with precipitation increasing over time in wine</cite>. Winemaking practices (microoxygenation, barrel aging) and phenolic composition (tannin/anthocyanin ratios) modulate these equilibria. <cite id="320002e8-0">Quercetin haze was delayed or prevented by microoxygenation and barrel maturation, consistent with stabilization via phenolic interactions</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Wines richer in tannins/anthocyanins showed higher soluble quercetin after storage, aligning with the hypothesis that macromolecules facilitate solubilization</cite>.

Practical implications: measuring “solubility” and interpreting results
- Free vs total: Directly measuring free quercetin requires equilibrium dialysis, size‑exclusion chromatography, or binding titrations; otherwise, absorbance‑based “solubility” reflects total quercetin species. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Anthocyanin–flavonol–flavanol interactions can be colorimetrically tracked, but antagonisms and synergies mean that apparent color/absorbance does not always equal free concentration</cite>. 
- Interpreting wine data: Wines that bind quercetin into complexes show higher “apparent solubility” and lower free quercetin; precipitation risk is concentration‑, pH‑, ethanol‑, and time‑dependent. <cite id="320002e8-0">Solubility was lower at 0 °C vs 18 °C, and anthocyanins maintained more quercetin in solution; the effect wanes over time</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Ethanol and pH influence quercetin solubility, but wine’s complex matrix can produce solubility different from simple solutions</cite>. 
- Condensed tannin additions: Small to moderate additions can increase apparent solubility by forming complexes and enhancing stabilization, but strong effects are more typical for hydrolysable tannins or quercetin; condensed tannins may reduce free quercetin while increasing the bound pool, with little direct anthocyanin copigmentation at typical wine concentrations. <cite id="b9844c0a-0">Hydrolysable tannins copigmented 2–4× more strongly than condensed tannins in model wine</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-4">Procyanidin B1/B2 showed weak immediate copigmentation, suggesting limited direct impact at typical levels but measurable shifts over storage</cite>.

Answering the definitional question
- Does “solubility” mean free dissolved concentration or apparent solubility including complexes? In most wine studies, “solubility” refers to apparent solubility—i.e., the total amount of quercetin and quercetin–phenolic complexes that remain in solution and contribute to color/spectral signals—because binding and copigmentation dominate phenolic behavior in red wine. <cite id="320002e8-0">Copigmentation with anthocyanins increases the apparent solubility of quercetin by preventing precipitation and keeping more quercetin in solution</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-0">High copigmentation constants for quercetin–anthocyanin complexes indicate that measured color/absorbance largely reflects bound species</cite>. 
- Effect of condensed tannins: Condensed tannins do not generally increase free quercetin; instead, they can increase the apparent solubility by binding quercetin and/or anthocyanins, forming mixed complexes that stay dissolved, thereby lowering free quercetin while increasing the total quercetin-related dissolved mass. At typical wine concentrations, direct copigmentation with anthocyanins by condensed tannins is modest, but their presence shifts equilibria toward more quercetin sequestration into complexes and can reduce precipitation risk up to a concentration threshold. <cite id="2af35bf7-4">Procyanidin additions showed weak immediate color effects but pronounced shifts during aging</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Higher anthocyanin/tannin matrices keep more quercetin dissolved and delay precipitation</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Deposition becomes significant once dissolved quercetin exceeds ~3 mg/L, with matrix interactions controlling nucleation and growth</cite>.

Caveats and uncertainties
- The net effect depends on phenolic profile (anthocyanin, flavanol, tannin levels), pH, ethanol, oxygen, and time; quercetin may initially bind to anthocyanins and later polymerize or form mixed tannin–anthocyanin–quercetin structures. <cite id="b9844c0a-3">Copigmentation decreases during storage while polymerized structures increase, altering wine colorants</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-4">Over storage, copigmented solutions shift toward lighter, more yellow hues, consistent with evolving complexes</cite>.

Summary
Condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins) do not generally increase the free aqueous concentration of quercetin, but they can increase quercetin’s apparent solubility by forming soluble complexes and copigmentation assemblies with other phenolics in wine matrices, thereby suppressing precipitation and shifting quercetin from free monomer toward bound species that remain in solution. In red wine, “solubility” is rarely a thermodynamic free-concentration question; it is typically an apparent measure of total quercetin-related species detectable spectrophotometrically or by binding equilibria, because noncovalent complexes with anthocyanins and tannins absorb differently and contribute to “in solution” mass without free quercetin monomer precipitating. <cite id="320002e8-0">Non‑covalent interactions with anthocyanins and wine phenolics can stabilize quercetin in solution and increase its apparent solubility</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Quercetin’s risk of precipitation depends on matrix composition, time, and concentration, with reports of a critical threshold around 3 mg/L and clear evidence that wine components modulate nucleation and growth via noncovalent interactions</cite>.

What “solubility” means in red wine
In wine chemistry, “solubility” of quercetin is often operationalized as the total amount “in solution” (free quercetin plus quercetin–phenolic complexes) rather than the thermodynamic solubility of the unbound flavonol. Spectrophotometric color indices and copigmentation metrics reflect total quercetin-related absorbance that arises from bound complexes, not just free quercetin. <cite id="2af35bf7-0">Copigmentation constants K1 for anthocyanin–quercetin complexes are on the order of 10^3 L/mol, indicating strong complex formation that contributes to color, whereas catechin and procyanidin interactions are weaker</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Experiments that spike quercetin into wine and track dissolution/precipitation show higher apparent solubility when anthocyanins and wine matrices are present, attributed to stabilizing complexes preventing quercetin precipitation</cite>. Because quercetin is relatively hydrophobic and phenolic matrices are complex, measurements in real wine differ from simple aqueous solubility and must account for binding to anthocyanins, tannins, acids, and metalloids. <cite id="320002e8-3">Quercetin’s intrinsic water solubility is low (μg/mL), but wine matrices and ethanol/pH modulate its apparent solubility and precipitation risk</cite>.

How condensed tannins affect quercetin
Mechanisms: binding, complexation, and copigmentation
Condensed tannins primarily act through noncovalent forces (π–π stacking, H-bonding, hydrophobic interactions) to complex phenolic chromophores and stabilize colored species. Direct copigmentation with anthocyanins by condensed tannins is generally less effective than with hydrolysable tannins or quercetin, but interactions can still occur and alter color expression and stability. <cite id="b9844c0a-0">In model wine, oenological tannins increased color (a*, decreased L* and b*), with hydrolysable tannins outperforming condensed tannins in copigmentation effectiveness by ~2–4×</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-4">Procyanidin dimers (B1/B2) showed weak copigmentation in model wine at typical concentrations, implying limited direct impact on color via copigmentation at physiologically relevant levels</cite>. When quercetin is present, it can participate in anthocyanin–quercetin–flavanol ternary complexes and act as a stabilizer over time, sometimes even suppressing catechin’s stabilizing role. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Quercetin‑3‑β‑D‑glucoside produced immediate copigmentation and greater stabilization over time; in the presence of quercetin, (+)‑catechin binding to malvidin was less effective, indicating quercetin–anthocyanin complexes can dominate and reduce catechin’s contribution</cite>.

Apparent solubility of quercetin in the presence of condensed tannins
Evidence from wine and model systems indicates that adding phenolic cofactors (including condensed tannins) raises the apparent solubility window for quercetin by forming soluble complexes, which delays or prevents free quercetin precipitation. <cite id="320002e8-0">A spike‑and‑store study showed that higher anthocyanin concentrations corresponded to higher quercetin concentrations remaining in solution, and that anthocyanin–quercetin copigmentation complexes prevent quercetin precipitation</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Subsequent work confirmed that hydrolysable tannins and wine matrices increase quercetin solubility via noncovalent interactions</cite>. Real‑wine correlations further support this: bound quercetin correlates with tannins and monomeric anthocyanins/flavanols, consistent with sequestration into complexes. <cite id="320002e8-0">Screening of Sangiovese wines found significant positive correlations between quercetin aglycone and anthocyanins, and between bound quercetin and tannins</cite>. At the same time, free quercetin can decrease over time as it binds to matrix components, and precipitation risk increases once dissolved quercetin exceeds a threshold (≈3 mg/L) and as tannin/anthocyanin levels decline with aging. <cite id="320002e8-0">Quercetin deposits were observed when solution content fell below ~3 mg/L, and the effect decreased over time as complexation shifted equilibria</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Deposits formed over time and increased above ~3 mg/L, with wine components modulating nucleation and growth via noncovalent interactions</cite>.

Condensed tannins vs hydrolysable tannins and quercetin: a hierarchy of effects
Quercetin itself is a stronger copigment and complex former than condensed tannins when interacting with anthocyanins, and even stronger than most flavanols; hydrolysable tannins (gallotannins/ellagitannins) often outperform condensed tannins in anthocyanin copigmentation in model wine. <cite id="b9844c0a-0">Hydrolysable tannins were 2–4× more effective copigments than condensed tannins in malvidin models, with effects that were dose‑ and pH/ethanol‑dependent</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-0">Anthocyanin–quercetin copigmentation had K1 ≈ 2900 ± 1300 L/mol, far exceeding catechin (≈90 ± 20 L/mol) and procyanidin dimers (≈330 ± 30 L/mol)</cite>. Thus, in the presence of quercetin, condensed tannins tend to bind to anthocyanins and/or to quercetin–anthocyanin complexes, potentially reducing free quercetin while increasing the apparent solubility (total bound + free) of quercetin‑related species. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Quercetin–anthocyanin complexes can dominate over catechin in stabilizing color over time, indicating that condensed tannins may bind to complexes and shift quercetin from free to bound pools</cite>.

Time, matrix composition, and concentration effects
Because quercetin’s solubility is matrix‑ and time‑dependent, the net effect of adding condensed tannins is not a simple increase in free quercetin. Instead, tannins can (i) form quercetin–tannin complexes that remain dissolved, increasing apparent solubility; (ii) drive anthocyanin–quercetin copigmentation that sequesters quercetin, lowering free quercetin; and (iii) contribute to long‑term precipitation risk if tannin levels decline or if dissolved quercetin exceeds ~3 mg/L. <cite id="320002e8-0">Higher anthocyanin concentrations maintained more quercetin in solution via copigmentation, but this effect diminished over time</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">A threshold around 3 mg/L marked the onset of significant deposit formation, with precipitation increasing over time in wine</cite>. Practical implications: measuring “solubility” and interpreting results
- Free vs total: Directly measuring free quercetin requires equilibrium dialysis, size‑exclusion chromatography, or binding titrations; otherwise, absorbance‑based “solubility” reflects total quercetin species. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Anthocyanin–flavonol–flavanol interactions can be colorimetrically tracked, but antagonisms and synergies mean that apparent color/absorbance does not always equal free concentration</cite>. 
- Interpreting wine data: Wines that bind quercetin into complexes show higher “apparent solubility” and lower free quercetin; precipitation risk is concentration‑, pH‑, ethanol‑, and time‑dependent. <cite id="320002e8-0">Solubility was lower at 0 °C vs 18 °C, and anthocyanins maintained more quercetin in solution; the effect wanes over time</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Ethanol and pH influence quercetin solubility, but wine’s complex matrix can produce solubility different from simple solutions</cite>. 
- Condensed tannin additions: Small to moderate additions can increase apparent solubility by forming complexes and enhancing stabilization, but strong effects are more typical for hydrolysable tannins or quercetin; condensed tannins may reduce free quercetin while increasing the bound pool, with little direct anthocyanin copigmentation at typical wine concentrations. <cite id="b9844c0a-0">Hydrolysable tannins copigmented 2–4× more strongly than condensed tannins in model wine</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-4">Procyanidin B1/B2 showed weak immediate copigmentation, suggesting limited direct impact at typical levels but measurable shifts over storage</cite>.

Answering the definitional question
- Does “solubility” mean free dissolved concentration or apparent solubility including complexes? In most wine studies, “solubility” refers to apparent solubility—i.e., the total amount of quercetin and quercetin–phenolic complexes that remain in solution and contribute to color/spectral signals—because binding and copigmentation dominate phenolic behavior in red wine. <cite id="320002e8-0">Copigmentation with anthocyanins increases the apparent solubility of quercetin by preventing precipitation and keeping more quercetin in solution</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-0">High copigmentation constants for quercetin–anthocyanin complexes indicate that measured color/absorbance largely reflects bound species</cite>. 
- Effect of condensed tannins: Condensed tannins do not generally increase free quercetin; instead, they can increase the apparent solubility by binding quercetin and/or anthocyanins, forming mixed complexes that stay dissolved, thereby lowering free quercetin while increasing the total quercetin-related dissolved mass. At typical wine concentrations, direct copigmentation with anthocyanins by condensed tannins is modest, but their presence shifts equilibria toward more quercetin sequestration into complexes and can reduce precipitation risk up to a concentration threshold. <cite id="2af35bf7-4">Procyanidin additions showed weak immediate color effects but pronounced shifts during aging</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Higher anthocyanin/tannin matrices keep more quercetin dissolved and delay precipitation</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Deposition becomes significant once dissolved quercetin exceeds ~3 mg/L, with matrix interactions controlling nucleation and growth</cite>.

Caveats and uncertainties
- The net effect depends on phenolic profile (anthocyanin, flavanol, tannin levels), pH, ethanol, oxygen, and time; quercetin may initially bind to anthocyanins and later polymerize or form mixed tannin–anthocyanin–quercetin structures. <cite id="b9844c0a-3">Copigmentation decreases during storage while polymerized structures increase, altering wine colorants</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-4">Over storage, copigmented solutions shift toward lighter, more yellow hues, consistent with evolving complexes</cite>. 
- Quantifying free vs bound quercetin requires equilibrium and speciation methods; many wine studies report total/complexed signals. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Multiple copigmentation combinations can produce synergistic or antagonistic effects, complicating interpretation of color-based solubility</cite>. 
- Future work that directly measures free quercetin vs total quercetin across condensed tannin concentrations, pH gradients, and aging would clarify the magnitude of free-concentration changes versus apparent solubility increases. <cite id="2af35bf7-2">Further studies are needed to strategically select flavonoid combinations and avoid antagonisms, and to understand mechanisms under varying pH, temperature, and sulfite conditions</cite>.

Bottom line
- In red wine, “solubility” of quercetin is best interpreted as apparent solubility (total quercetin plus complexes), not free monomer concentration. <cite id="320002e8-0">Anthocyanin–quercetin complexes maintain quercetin in solution and raise apparent solubility</cite><cite id="2af35bf7-0">High copigmentation constants indicate strong complexation</cite>.

The strength and direction of effect depend on matrix composition, phenolic profiles, and time. <cite id="b9844c0a-0">Hydrolysable tannins are typically stronger copigments than condensed tannins</cite><cite id="320002e8-0">Wine matrices and anthocyanins stabilize quercetin and increase apparent solubility</cite><cite id="320002e8-3">Deposition risk rises above ~3 mg/L and over time, modulated by matrix interactions</cite>.

Title: Copigmentation of Malvidin-3-O-Monoglucoside by Oenological Tannins: Incidence on Wine Model Color in Function of Botanical Origin, pH and Ethanol Content
Snippet: The effect of the botanical origin, pH level and ethanol content of different oenological tannins on the color of malvidin-3-O-monoglucoside solution, including their effectiveness as copigments, was studied. Briefly, a model wine solution (4 g/L of tartaric acid, pH 3.5 and 12% ethanol) containing 50 mg/L of malvidin-3-O-monoglucoside was prepared and supplemented with 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 g/L of commercial tannins using (−)-epicatechin as reference control copigment. Six additional model wine solutions (12% ethanol at pH 3.1, 3.5 or 3.9, and 10%, 12% or 14% ethanol at pH 3.5) were prepared as previously described. Samples were stored under airtight conditions. After a week the full absorbance spectrum in the visible range (400–800 nm) was measured and CIELAB color space was determined. These measurements, including an increase in a* (redness), a decrease in b* (yellowness) and a decrease in L* (lightness), indicated that all oenological tannins had a clear positive effect on color copigmentation. Moreover, hydrolysable tannins appeared to be better copigments than condensed tannins as the copigmentation effectiveness (Cp) was found to be between two to four times higher. The effects of these tannins were dose-dependent because a higher addition resulted in a greater impact on copigmentation. In general, an increase in pH and ethanol content resulted in a decrease of the effect of tannins on color. Independent of intrinsic wine conditions, hydrolysable tannins, more specifically gallotannin, remain the most effective in increasing red wine color. These results prove that supplementation with oenological tannins, especially hydrolysable tannins, could be an interesting tool for the improvement of the red wine color.

Title: Copigmentation of Malvidin-3-O-Monoglucoside by Oenological Tannins: Incidence on Wine Model Color in Function of Botanical Origin, pH and Ethanol Content
Snippet: The thirty-six oenological tannins were used to determine the influence of the botanical origin on the copigmentation effect. A model wine solution (12% ethanol, 4 g/L of tartaric acid and adjusted at pH 3.5) was prepared and supplemented with 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 g/L of each of the thirty-six commercial tannins and (−)-epicatechin (copigments). The (−)-epicatechin was used as reference standard. Simultaneously, solutions containing 50 mg/L of malvidin-3-O-monoglucoside (pigment) and 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 g/L of commercial tannins or (−)-epicatechin were prepared to reach copigment/pigment ratios of 2, 4 and 8 respectively. Finally, a solution containing only the malvidin was prepared as positive control. Then, 1.5 mL of each solution was placed in Eppendorf tubes and maintained under airtight conditions. A week later, the full absorbance spectrum in the visible range (400-800 nm) was measured to determine the CIELAB color space and the effectiveness of copigmentation (Cp).

Title: A review of the current knowledge of red wine colour
Snippet: Copigmentation depends on the structure of the anthocyanins and particularly on the structure of the copigments. Comparing the potential of flavonols (like quercetin) and flavan-3-ols to act as copigments, the first group is a better choice since it generally has a planar polyphenolic nucleus capable of forming π-stacking with the anthocyanin planar chromophore (Mistry et al., 1991;Cruz et al., 2010). Such hydrophobic complexation displaces the equilibria towards the formation of more flavylium forms of anthocyanins. Nevertheless, red wine is more concentrated in flavan-3-ols than in flavonols and the contact with anthocyanins is inevitable (Neveu et al., 2010). Several authors performed copigmentation studies in model solutions with several cofactors including (epi)catechin, (epi)gallocatechin, procyanidins, prodelphinidins, myricetin, quercetin and phenolic acids such as caffeic acid and p-coumaric acid. Malvidin-3-O-glucoside, being the main anthocyanin present in red wines, is usually the chosen pigment for copigmentation studies (Teixeira et al., 2013;Darias-Martin et al., 2001). Among flavan-3-ols, (-)-epicatechin is a better copigment than (+)-catechin due to its C ring conformation, allowing it to be approximately coplanar (Brouillard, 1991;Liao et al., 1992) ; the presence of a pyrogallol group in the B ring slightly increases the copimentation potential (Teixeira et al., 2013); procyanidin dimers with C-4C-6 interflavanic linkages seem to be better copigments than their respective C-4C-8 dimers; and galloylation at C-3 also increases the copigmentation effect (Berké et al., 2005).

Title: Influence of oenological tannins on malvidin-3-O-monoglucoside copigmentation in a model wine solution
Snippet: More recently, it has been reported that anthocyanins can also react with ellagitannins to form new pigments (Chassaing et al., 2010). 

It is generally accepted that copigmentation is responsible for a substantial proportion (32-43%) of the color of young red wines (Hermosín-Gutiérrez et al., 2005). It has also been suggested that copigmentation may be the first step in the formation of covalent bonds between anthocyanins and flavanols (flavan-3-ol monomers and proanthocyanidins), thus creating new anthocyanin-derived pigments either directly or through the participation of ethanal (Francia-Aricha et al., 1997;de Freitas et al., 2017). Indeed, during storage or aging, copigmentation decreases and the concentration of polymerized structures increases, with consequent changes in the wine (Brouillard and Dangles, 1994;Gutiérrez et al., 2005;Liao et al., 1992). 

In previous studies, some researchers have shown the effectiveness as copigments of different pure phenolic compounds in model wine solutions. However, to our knowledge very little scientific information exists about the effectiveness as copigments of these commercial tannins, which are evidently not pure substances. As previously mentioned, the use of commercial oenological tannins is a common practice in modern winemaking, and for this reason the OIV is now reconsidering the properties of oenological tannins in order to rewrite the OIV International Oenological Codex and authorize their use for other purposes. Considering all the above, the aim of the present research was to study the effect of diverse oenological tannins on the color of the anthocyanin malvidin-3-O-monoglucoside in a model wine solution, and to propose a new index to measure the actual effectiveness as copigments of the different commercial products.

Title: Influence of oenological tannins on malvidin-3-O-monoglucoside copigmentation in a model wine solution
Snippet: Table 3 summarizes the results for copigmentation index values of (-)-epicatechin and the different commercial tannins investigated. The copigmentation index illustrates simply the effectiveness of the different commercial tannins to improve wine color, which, as discussed, is mainly due to the copigmentation phenomenon. 

According to the index, on day 1 the best copigment is (-)-epicatechin and ellagitannin, followed in decreasing order by gallotannin, seed tannin, quebracho tannin and skin tannin. However, on day 7 some interesting differences can be observed. First, the copigmentation index of (-)-epicatechin and, to a lesser extent, quebracho tannin and ellagitannin, decrease significantly, suggesting that the copigmentation effect decreases or that malvidin-3-O-glucoside reacts to form new compounds with a lesser contribution to the color. In contrast, the copigmentation index of seed tannin, skin tannin and gallotannin increases significantly, probably because the staking structures responsible for the copigmentation effect need time to form completely or because new pigments with a greater contribution to the color are formed (at least in the case of the case of seed tannin).
